1.title: Level 1 - Foundations
1.blurb: Clear basics. Spot obvious false comfort.

items.text: If the code runs without crashing, that alone proves it is ready for paying users.
A bug that only shows up once a week is still worth tracking down before a release.
Copying a stack-overflow snippet into production without reading it is fine if tests pass later.
Clear names for variables and functions help the next person (including future you) understand the code.
If a feature works on your laptop, it will automatically work the same way on a customer's machine.
Writing down what a tricky function is supposed to do can save more time than jumping straight into edits.
Deleting unused code is riskier than leaving dead code forever, so dead code should never be removed.
A failing test that used to pass is a signal to investigate, not a signal to delete the test.
Shipping a half-finished feature behind a flag can be safer than shipping it fully wired for everyone.
If a change is small, reviewing it is optional even when it touches money or passwords.
Logging errors with enough context to reproduce them is part of writing maintainable software.
More lines of code always means higher quality.

2.title: Level 2 - Trade-offs
2.blurb: Two good-looking options; only one is sound.

items.text: If a hotfix works in production, skipping a regression check on the related path is justified by urgency forever.
Preferring a boring, readable fix over a clever one-liner is often the stronger long-term call.
When two bugs appear related, fixing only the one in the ticket is always enough.
A failing CI check you do not understand should block merge until it is explained or fixed.
Commenting out assertions to get green builds is a valid definition of done.
Reproducing a bug with the smallest input before editing code usually saves time.
If the type checker is quiet, runtime null cases can be ignored.
Naming a function for what it returns (or does) beats naming it for how it used to work.
Copying credentials into a local script for speed is fine if you delete the file later someday.
A pull request that explains the risk of the change helps reviewers catch what tests miss.

3.title: Level 3 - Failure modes
3.blurb: What breaks under load, time, or bad incentives.

items.text: A race that only appears under load can still be a release blocker even if local runs look clean.
If retries hide intermittent failures, the underlying flake can be treated as solved.
Logging enough context to rebuild the failing input is part of making production debuggable.
Swallowing exceptions to keep the UI calm is always better than surfacing a clear error.
Idempotent handlers reduce pain when a message or request is delivered twice.
Time-dependent bugs that only fail near midnight UTC are not real bugs.
Feature flags that never get cleaned up become a complexity tax on every future change.
If the happy path is covered, permission and empty-state paths can wait indefinitely.
Pinning dependency versions you actually tested reduces surprise breaks from floating ranges.
A green deploy means user-visible correctness is guaranteed across all regions.

4.title: Level 4 - Precedents & traps
4.blurb: Industry-familiar traps dressed as best practice.

items.text: Precedent trap: many outages start with a small config change that skipped the same review as code.
If staging data is fake and tiny, a green staging run fully proves production scale behavior.
Hotfixes that bypass tests should still get a follow-up that restores the safety net.
Deleting a flaky test is better than quarantining it with an owner and a fix date.
Shared mutable globals that work in a single-threaded mental model often fail under concurrency.
If the ticket says P0, skipping a second pair of eyes on auth code is the professional norm.
Writing down the rollback steps before a risky migrate is cheaper than inventing them mid-incident.
A library upgrade that only changes a patch version can never affect behavior.
When logs contradict the user's report, both can be true until you reconcile clocks and versions.
Ship-first-fix-later is a sustainable strategy for money-moving code.

5.title: Level 5 - Edge judgment
5.blurb: Subtle cases where polite process still fails the user.

items.text: A change that is locally correct can still be wrong if it violates an unstated multi-service contract.
If peers praise cleverness, that alone outweighs maintainability for production code.
Silent data repair jobs can hide corruption until the repair itself fails.
When two fixes both pass tests, picking the one that reduces future branching cost is often wiser.
Observability debt is optional if the team is small enough to SSH into boxes.
A partial outage that only hits 2% of users can still deserve the same rigor as a total outage.
If a workaround is temporary, leaving no ticket or expiry makes it permanent by default.
Correctness under cancellation (user hits stop) is irrelevant for request handlers.
When requirements conflict, making the conflict explicit beats silently favoring the loudest stakeholder.
Once code is merged, questioning the design in review notes is too late to ever matter.

1.title: Level 1 - Foundations
1.blurb: Clear basics. Spot obvious false comfort.

items.text: A design that is hard to change later can cost more than the time saved by shipping it quickly today.
If an API has no documented failure modes, callers can safely assume it never fails.
Ownership of a service includes knowing how to roll back a bad deploy.
Adding a new dependency has no long-term cost if it solves today's ticket.
A pull request description that explains why the change exists helps reviewers judge risk.
If production looks fine in one region, multi-region behavior can be assumed identical.
Feature flags and gradual rollout are tools for reducing blast radius, not only for marketing experiments.
Skipping monitoring for a new endpoint is fine because users will email if anything breaks.
Race conditions can appear only under load, so a quiet local run does not prove concurrency is safe.
Backwards-compatible API changes matter less than shipping the new field name you prefer.
Incident write-ups that name the trigger and the fix help the team avoid the same failure.
Technical debt is always a personal failure of the last engineer who touched the file.

2.title: Level 2 - Trade-offs
2.blurb: Two good-looking options; only one is sound.

items.text: Shipping a dual-write 'just for a week' without a delete plan usually becomes permanent complexity.
If the p50 latency looks great, a brutal p99 can still make the product feel broken for many users.
Choosing eventual consistency without saying who resolves conflicts is a complete data design.
A canary that only watches CPU can miss a correctness bug that burns a slice of users.
When a library is popular on GitHub, skipping a threat review of its update path is fine.
Contract tests between services catch breakages that unit tests inside one repo miss.
If the ticket is small, expanding the blast radius of a shared module needs no extra caution.
Naming the SLO and the error budget before a reliability push keeps trade-offs honest.
A manual runbook step that only one person can perform is a hidden single point of failure.
Green unit tests prove the deploy is safe across every region and traffic shape.

3.title: Level 3 - Failure modes
3.blurb: What breaks under load, time, or bad incentives.

items.text: A timeout shorter than a dependency's p99 will create false failures under ordinary load.
Unbounded retries against a sick dependency can amplify into a self-inflicted outage.
Caching without a clear invalidation story can serve wrong data longer than the bug that wrote it.
A circuit breaker that opens forever with no recovery path is still a complete resilience design.
Schema migrations that lock large tables can be correct SQL and still take production down.
If the happy-path SLA is green, error-budget burn on a minority path can be ignored.
Dual-writing to two stores without reconciliation often creates silent divergence.
Load tests that only use perfect synthetic data fully predict messy real traffic.
Runbooks that name the first three checks beat tribal knowledge during pages.
A blue/green deploy with no smoke checks is as safe as one with smoke checks.

4.title: Level 4 - Precedents & traps
4.blurb: Industry-familiar traps dressed as best practice.

items.text: Precedent: many postmortems cite a config flag flipped without the same review as code.
If on-call is quiet for a month, removing alerts is the right reliability strategy.
Capacity planning needs real usage signals, not only the day-one estimate.
Shared databases across unrelated teams always reduce coordination forever.
A breaking API change with no deprecation window taxes every unknown client.
If the vendor SLA is 99.99%, your product SLA can ignore your own retry and queue design.
Shadow traffic (dark launch) can reveal behavioral diffs that staging never showed.
Blame-first incident reviews improve long-term system safety more than blameless ones.
Gradual percentage rollouts catch classes of bugs that unit tests miss.
If staging shares production credentials, that is a convenience worth keeping.

5.title: Level 5 - Edge judgment
5.blurb: Subtle cases where polite process still fails the user.

items.text: A change can pass every test and still violate a multi-team ownership boundary that users depend on.
Optimizing average latency while ignoring a toxic tail can still ruin a subset of users.
If leadership wants a date, silently cutting safety checks is the professional way to hit it.
Making failure modes visible in the API often beats returning a vague 500 forever.
A successful migration with no rollback rehearsal is proven disaster-ready.
When two services disagree about a fact, the system needs an ownership rule, not hope.
Quiet deletes of deprecated fields without consumer checks are safe if the field felt unused.
Error budgets exist to trade speed and safety explicitly, not to shame individuals.
If a dependency is cheap, coupling your critical path to it has no strategic cost.
The hardest engineering judgment is sometimes refusing a path the org cannot operate.
